passage: On the balcony of their flat in Mumbai, Farida landed on the longest snake and slid all the way from 98 to 7. Uma rolled a six and won. Farida's face went red. She swept the counters off the board. "Not fair!" She stomped to the corner and sat with her arms crossed, breathing loudly through her nose. Uma waited. After a while Farida's shoulders came down. She picked up a counter from the floor and brought it back. "One more game," she said. "I'm green this time."

qa.q: Which square did Farida slide down from?
qa.a: She slid from 98 all the way to 7.

qa.q: What does Farida's loud breathing, followed by her shoulders coming down, show?
qa.a: She was angry and disappointed, but she calmed herself in the corner instead of staying upset.

qa.q: How could an adult help Farida the next time she loses?
qa.a: Name the feeling, like "That snake felt so unfair!", let her take a short break, then welcome her back without a lecture.

qa.q: What was it like for Uma to wait?
qa.a: She may have been startled when the counters flew, but her patience gave Farida room to recover and play again.

grounding: It shows a child's brief angry outburst after losing a game and her own recovery within minutes.

passage:
"My tower! It fell!" Arohi kicked a block.
"Oh no," said Mehak. "It was so tall."
"I hate blocks! I'm never playing again!" Arohi flopped onto the rug, face down.
Mehak sat beside her and said nothing for a bit. Then: "Want to count to five with me?"
"No." A pause. "One, two..." muffled into the rug.
"Three, four, five."
Arohi rolled over, eyes wet. "It had a flag on top."
"We can make a flag again. Want the wide blocks at the bottom this time?"
Arohi sat up and grabbed a wide one.

qa.q: What did Arohi say had been on top of her tower?
qa.a: She said it had a flag on top.

qa.q: Why did Arohi say "I hate blocks"?
qa.a: She was upset and disappointed that her tall tower fell, and the words came out of that frustration. 😢

qa.q: Which of Mehak's choices helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting quietly and offering to count gave Arohi time to calm down without being told off, and the wide-block idea gave her a way back.

qa.q: How might Mehak have felt when Arohi flopped face down?
qa.a: She may have felt a bit helpless at first, but she stayed calm, which kept the upset small.

grounding: It shows a child recovering from a small disappointment within minutes, helped by counting and a new plan.

passage: Teacher's note, KG-B, written by Indu. Musical chairs today. Elizabeth was out in the second round. Last month this would have meant a long cry under the table. Today she stamped once, said "Aww!" loudly, and her lip trembled. Then she took three big breaths, the way we practised with "balloon belly," and went to sit on the cheering bench. By the fourth round she was clapping for her friends. I told her I saw her breathing. She grinned. I will share the balloon breath with her parents. 👍

qa.q: How many big breaths did Elizabeth take?
qa.a: She took three big breaths.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth's trembling lip followed by clapping suggest?
qa.a: She felt disappointed about being out, but managed the feeling and even began enjoying her friends' game.

qa.q: Why is Indu's plan to share the balloon breath with the parents useful?
qa.a: Elizabeth can use the same calming trick at home, so the skill gets practised in more places.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's friends experience the change?
qa.a: Instead of a long upset, they get her cheers from the bench, which makes the game happier for everyone.

grounding: It shows a child bouncing back from losing a game with a practised calming breath rather than a long meltdown.

passage: In the lane outside the kirana shop, Ojas lost his last marble to Chetan. His lip pushed out and his fists clenched. 'Not fair!' He kicked the dust once. Chetan shrugged and held up the marble. Ojas turned away, breathing hard, and stared at the buffalo tied nearby. After a moment he turned back. 'Play again? I'll win this time.' Chetan grinned and set the marbles down.

qa.q: Where were the boys playing marbles?
qa.a: They were playing in the lane outside the kirana shop.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he kicked the dust?
qa.a: He was angry and disappointed at losing his last marble.

qa.q: What helped Ojas recover without a long meltdown?
qa.a: Turning away and looking at the buffalo gave him a short break to breathe, so he could calm down and try again.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Ojas coming back to play?
qa.a: He would likely be glad the game can go on, rather than having to deal with a long sulk.

grounding: Illustrates a child recovering from a lost game after brief frustration, in a small-town lane.

passage: At the kitchen table in Valencia, Dalia's counter slid down the longest snake, all the way back to the start. 'Noooo!' She threw her dice on the floor and crossed her arms. Santiago, her big brother, waited. Dalia huffed and stared at the ceiling. Then she climbed off her chair, picked up the dice and plonked it back. 'Fine. I'm still playing.' Two turns later, she hit a ladder and cheered.

qa.q: Where did Dalia's counter slide back to?
qa.a: It slid all the way back to the start.

qa.q: What was Dalia feeling when she crossed her arms?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and cross about losing her progress in the game.

qa.q: What did Santiago's waiting give Dalia?
qa.a: It gave her space to calm down on her own instead of being scolded or rushed.

qa.q: What would change if Santiago had teased her for throwing the dice?
qa.a: She might have grown angrier and stopped playing, turning a short upset into a longer meltdown.

grounding: Shows a young child bouncing back from a setback in a game without a prolonged meltdown, in Spain.

passage: At the sports club's under-six race, Saurabh came fourth. He stamped his foot and threw his cap on the grass. "Not fair!" Coach Amandeep knelt beside him. "You're cross. Big breath with me?" They breathed in and out together, twice. Saurabh picked up his cap. When the winner walked past, he mumbled, "Well done." Then he asked, "Can I race again next week?"

qa.q: What place did Saurabh come in the race?
qa.a: He came fourth.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he threw his cap?
qa.a: He was angry and disappointed about not winning.

qa.q: What did Coach Amandeep do that helped Saurabh recover?
qa.a: Coach Amandeep named his feeling and breathed with him, which calmed him quickly.

qa.q: How might the winner feel when Saurabh says "Well done"?
qa.a: Pleased and a little surprised to be congratulated by someone who was upset a moment ago.

grounding: Shows a young child recovering from losing a race after a short outburst, with a coach's help.

passage: I'm Anirban, Tenzin's big brother. We were playing snakes and ladders, and Tenzin, who is five, was nearly at the top when he landed on the longest snake. He slid all the way down to eight. His face went red and he pushed the board. I thought he'd cry for an hour, like last year. But he hugged his knees, took a few breaths and said, "One more roll." He lost anyway. He shrugged and asked to play again.

qa.q: Which square did Tenzin slide down to?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: What might Tenzin have felt when he landed on the longest snake?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated and angry, since his face went red and he pushed the board.

qa.q: How could Anirban support Tenzin when he loses?
qa.a: Stay calm, wait while he breathes, and praise him for trying again.

qa.q: How does Anirban see Tenzin's reaction compared with last year?
qa.a: He is surprised and impressed that Tenzin calmed himself instead of crying for an hour.

grounding: Shows a young child calming himself after a disappointing game, seen by an older brother.

passage: Monday: Rehana, five, couldn't fit the last puzzle piece and swept the whole puzzle onto the floor, screaming for ten minutes. Her mother Manjula sat nearby. Wednesday: the piece didn't fit again. Rehana threw it, then cried, then came to sit in Manjula's lap. Saturday: she got stuck again. She put the piece down, hugged her cushion, and said, "I'm cross." After a minute she turned the piece round and it clicked in.

qa.q: How long did Rehana scream on Monday?
qa.a: For ten minutes.

qa.q: What does Rehana hugging her cushion and saying "I'm cross" suggest?
qa.a: She felt angry but was learning to soothe herself and name the feeling instead of melting down.

qa.q: Which choice by Manjula helped over the week?
qa.a: Sitting nearby calmly each time, so Rehana felt safe enough to learn to settle herself.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel on Saturday?
qa.a: Relieved and proud to see Rehana handle her frustration on her own.

grounding: Shows a young child's reactions to frustration shortening over a week until she can soothe herself.

passage: It was almost bedtime, and Reena, six, was one move from winning ludo when Anjali, her mother, cut her last token. Reena's face went red. She swept the board, and pieces flew. "Not fair!" Anjali didn't shout. "You're really cross. Let's do dragon breaths." Reena breathed out hard three times, like fire. Her fists opened. "Can we play once more tomorrow?" "Yes. And you can pick up the pieces now." Grumbling a little, Reena picked them up.

qa.q: What did Reena do when her token was cut?
qa.a: She swept the board and the pieces flew.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling when her face went red?
qa.a: Reena felt angry and disappointed at losing so close to winning.

qa.q: How did Anjali help Reena calm down?
qa.a: She named the feeling, did dragon breaths with her, and offered another game tomorrow while asking her to tidy up.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when Reena asks to play tomorrow?
qa.a: Anjali probably felt relieved and proud that Reena calmed down quickly.

grounding: Close to bedtime, a six-year-old loses a game, erupts, and recovers with her mother's calm help.

passage: In the week before Christmas in Aizawl, Lalremsiami, five, spent all afternoon cutting a paper star. When she pulled it off the table, one point tore. She threw the scissors down and stamped her foot, tears coming. Rukmini Aunty, her neighbour, watched from the doorway and waited. Lalremsiami hugged her knees and hummed a carol under her breath, rocking. After a minute she wiped her face and said, "I'll stick it." She taped the point back on, crooked, and hung it anyway.

qa.q: What tore on Lalremsiami's star?
qa.a: One point.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt frustrated and upset that her star tore after all her work.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami do to soothe herself?
qa.a: She hugged her knees, hummed a carol and rocked, then chose to fix the star with tape.

qa.q: How might Rukmini Aunty feel watching from the doorway?
qa.a: Rukmini Aunty probably felt impressed and relieved that Lalremsiami calmed herself without help.

grounding: In the week before Christmas, a five-year-old recovers from a torn paper star by soothing herself.

passage:
"I lost again!" Hafsa, five, pushed the carrom striker away. Rain had kept them inside all week.
"You nearly got the queen," said Kashish, her big sister.
"I never win!" Hafsa's chin wobbled.
"Want to throw the cushion first?"
Hafsa threw it at the wall. Thump. Then she sat on it. "Still cross."
"Okay. Count the raindrops on the window with me. Ten."
Hafsa counted slowly. By seven she was smiling.
"Again?"
"Only if I go first."
"Deal."

qa.q: What had kept them inside all week?
qa.a: Rain.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling when her chin wobbled?
qa.a: Hafsa felt frustrated and disappointed at losing again.

qa.q: How did Kashish help Hafsa recover?
qa.a: She offered a safe way to let out anger, then a calm counting activity, and a fair next game.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Hafsa asks to play again?
qa.a: Kashish probably felt pleased and relieved that her sister bounced back.

grounding: During a rainy week indoors, a big sister helps a five-year-old recover from losing at carrom.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Christmas party.

Ojas was out in the first round of musical chairs. He stamped his foot and shouted, "Not fair!"

Then he stopped, took a big breath like we practise, and sat on the side bench. After a minute he clapped for the others.

When the next game started, he joined in. — Sharmila

qa.q: In which round was Ojas out?
qa.a: Ojas was out in the first round of musical chairs.

qa.q: How did Ojas feel when he was out?
qa.a: Ojas felt angry and disappointed, stamping his foot and shouting "Not fair!"

qa.q: What helped Ojas recover?
qa.a: Taking a big breath like they practise, sitting aside for a minute, then joining the next game.

qa.q: How might Sharmila feel seeing Ojas clap for the others?
qa.a: Sharmila was likely proud of how he calmed himself.

grounding: At a Christmas party, a child recovers from losing musical chairs by breathing and rejoining the fun.

passage:
During Makar Sankranti in the village near Patna, Nitin and Arnab played marbles under the neem tree.

Arnab won all of Nitin's marbles.

Nitin's lip wobbled. He kicked the dust. Then he hummed a little song under his breath, the way his Dadi did when she was cross.

After a while he said, "One more game. I'll win this time."

Arnab gave him back two marbles to start.

qa.q: Where did Nitin and Arnab play marbles?
qa.a: They played under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel when he lost all his marbles?
qa.a: Nitin felt upset and frustrated, his lip wobbling as he kicked the dust.

qa.q: What did Nitin do to calm himself?
qa.a: He hummed a little song under his breath, like his Dadi, and then asked for another game.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel giving back two marbles?
qa.a: Arnab was probably feeling kind and fair, wanting Nitin to keep playing.

grounding: During Sankranti, a child soothes himself after losing at marbles and tries again instead of melting down.

passage:
The first snow in Riga was sticky and perfect. Nkechi, five, built a snowman with Olga, her nanny.

Just as she put on the carrot nose, the head rolled off and broke.

Nkechi's face crumpled. She sat down in the snow and cried.

Olga sat beside her. "That's so disappointing."

Nkechi cried for a minute, then wiped her nose on her mitten. "Let's make it smaller this time."

qa.q: What happened when Nkechi put on the carrot nose?
qa.a: The head rolled off and broke.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel when the snowman's head broke?
qa.a: Nkechi felt disappointed and upset, crying in the snow.

qa.q: How did Olga help Nkechi recover?
qa.a: She sat with her and named her feeling, giving Nkechi time to calm down.

qa.q: How might Olga feel when Nkechi suggested making it smaller?
qa.a: Olga was probably pleased and proud that Nkechi bounced back.

grounding: In the first snow, a child recovers from the disappointment of a broken snowman with her nanny's calm support.

passage: At the community centre's Holi party, the children played musical chairs. When the music stopped, Sarita slid onto the last chair and Binita was out. Binita stamped her foot, and her lip wobbled. She marched to the corner, squeezed her fists, then sat hugging her knees and blowing slow breaths, like blowing out birthday candles. Sarita called, "Binita, come be the music person!" After a minute, Binita wiped her eyes, walked over, and pressed play. By the next round she was grinning as she stopped the music.

qa.q: Who got the last chair?
qa.a: Sarita slid onto the last chair.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when she stamped her foot?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and angry at being out of the game.

qa.q: What helped Binita calm down, and what could an adult add?
qa.a: Slow breaths and a little time alone helped; an adult could quietly name her feeling and praise her for coming back. 👍

qa.q: How might Sarita feel when Binita comes over to press play?
qa.a: Sarita is probably relieved and pleased to have Binita back in the game.

grounding: Shows a young child recovering from losing a party game by calming herself instead of melting down.
